nameStory: The 'bean' in bean goose comes from this bird's love of eating beans and other agricultural crops during migration and winter. The 'tundra' part refers to where these geese breed - the treeless, windswept tundra of northern Siberia. Their scientific name 'serrirostris' means 'saw-billed,' referring to the serrated edges along their bill that help them grip slippery vegetation.
description: The Tundra Bean Goose is a large, brownish-gray goose that's an extremely rare visitor to New England from its breeding grounds in Siberian tundra. These hefty birds are about the size of a Canada Goose, with a distinctive orange-yellow bill marked by black patches. They have a somewhat shaggy appearance with darker brown heads and necks, and lighter grayish-brown bodies with pale edges on their wing feathers. Their legs are bright orange, making them stand out among other geese.

idTips.label: Bill Pattern
idTips.description: Orange-yellow bill with bold black markings near the tip and base - looks almost painted on compared to the more uniform bills of other geese

idTips.label: Orange Legs
idTips.description: Bright orange legs and feet that look almost artificial in their intensity, especially visible when walking on mudflats or grass

idTips.label: Body Coloring
idTips.description: Rich chocolate-brown head and neck with a grayish-brown body that has a slightly shaggy, unkempt appearance compared to sleeker geese

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: In flight, shows pale gray wing coverts with darker flight feathers, creating a two-toned appearance on the wings

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Stocky build similar to Canada Goose but with a shorter, thicker neck and more compact appearance overall

habitat: In New England, Tundra Bean Geese are most likely spotted in agricultural areas with harvested grain fields, coastal marshes, and large freshwater bodies during migration periods. They prefer open areas where they can feed on waste grain and aquatic vegetation, often associating with flocks of Canada Geese or other waterfowl. Look for them in places like Plum Island, Massachusetts, or Connecticut River valley farmlands.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare spring migrants may appear in March-April, usually mixed in with Canada Goose flocks in agricultural fields or coastal areas.
seasonality.summer: Not present in New England during summer months as they're busy breeding on the Siberian tundra thousands of miles away.
seasonality.fall: Most likely season to spot one, typically October-November, when lost migrants may appear during peak waterfowl migration.
seasonality.winter: Occasional winter records exist, usually of individuals that have joined Canada Goose flocks and linger at unfrozen water bodies.

funFact: Tundra Bean Geese and their close relatives the Taiga Bean Geese split apart as separate species 2.5 million years ago, but then met up again about 60,000 years ago and started interbreeding - making them one of nature's most dramatic examples of a species reunion after eons apart!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Greater White-fronted Goose, but Tundra Bean Goose lacks the distinctive white patch around the bill base and black belly bars. Remember: 'Bean geese have clean bellies, White-fronts have barred bellies.' Also distinguished from Greylag Goose by the orange (not pink) bill and legs.
contextualKnowledge: There's ongoing taxonomic confusion about bean geese - some authorities consider Tundra and Taiga Bean Geese as one species, while others split them. In North America, they're officially recognized as separate species, which is why you might see conflicting information in different field guides or websites about 'bean geese' in general.
compareHints: Compared to other grey geese in its genus, Tundra Bean Goose lacks the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Goose and the distinctive bill pattern of Pink-footed Goose. It's much browner overall than the paler Greylag Goose and significantly larger than Ross's Goose. The orange bill and legs are key features that separate it from most other geese in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Greater White-fronted Goose which has a white forehead patch and orange legs, Snow Geese are predominantly white all over with black wingtips.
Among the grey geese in its genus, Greylag Geese lack the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Geese and aren't pure white like Snow Geese.
Unlike Snow Geese which are mostly white or very pale, Greater White-fronted Geese are brown and gray with distinctive belly markings.
Among the grey geese, Pink-footed Geese are smaller and more compact than Greylag Geese, lack the white forehead of Greater White-fronted Geese, and have much pinker legs than any of their relatives.
Compared to Snow Geese in the same genus, Ross's Geese are significantly smaller with proportionally smaller, cleaner bills lacking black edges.
Among grey geese, Swan Goose is unmistakable due to its exceptionally long neck and orange bill.
